white-collar = relating to office or professional work rather than manual labour
blue-collar = relating to manual or industrial work, often paid by the hour
public sector = the part of the economy run by government, such as schools and hospitals
private sector = businesses owned by individuals or companies, not by the state
third sector = charities, social enterprises and other not-for-profit organisations
government official = a person employed by the state to run public administration
knowledge worker = someone whose main capital is expertise, analysis or design rather than physical labour
manufacturing industry = the sector that makes physical goods in factories
service industry = the sector that provides services rather than goods, such as retail or hospitality
gig economy = work sold in short tasks via apps, with little job security
labour market = the supply of and demand for paid work in an economy
workforce = all the people available for or engaged in work in a place
skilled labour = workers trained in a trade or technical craft
unskilled work = jobs that need little formal training on day one
manual labour = work done mainly with the hands and body
clerical job = office work such as filing, data entry and correspondence
middle management = managers between senior leaders and front-line staff
senior management = the group of directors and heads who set strategy
board of directors = the group legally responsible for governing a company
chief executive = the highest-ranking manager running a company day to day
line manager = the person you report to in the everyday hierarchy
human resources = the department that hires, pays and supports staff
professional body = an organisation that sets standards and entry rules for a profession
skilled trade = a practical occupation learnt through apprenticeship, such as plumbing
shortlist = the small group of applicants chosen for the last stage of recruitment
headhunter = a recruiter paid to approach people already in work for a vacancy
probation period = the first months in a job when either side may end it more easily
job description = an official outline of duties, seniority and working conditions
person specification = the skills, qualifications and traits an employer says it wants
aptitude test = a timed test of reasoning, numbers or language used in recruitment
psychometric testing = questionnaires that claim to measure personality or ability for hiring
assessment centre = a recruitment day of tasks, tests and interviews used to compare candidates
panel interview = an interview conducted by several people at once
competency-based interview = an interview that asks for evidence of skills through past examples
background check = enquiries into identity, qualifications or criminal record before hiring
work permit = official permission for a foreign national to take a job
job offer = a formal proposal of employment, usually in writing
turn down an offer = to refuse a job or contract that has been proposed
recruitment agency = a firm paid to find candidates for employers
speculative application = contacting an employer who has not advertised a vacancy
networking = building professional contacts who may share information or openings
transferable skills = abilities useful in more than one job or sector
soft skills = interpersonal abilities such as communication, teamwork and empathy
hard skills = teachable technical abilities such as coding, accounting or welding
onboarding = the structured process of settling a new employee into the organisation
induction programme = a planned introduction to rules, people and systems at the start of a job
job shadowing = following an experienced worker to learn what the role involves
graduate scheme = a structured traineeship for people with degrees, rotating through departments
internship = a short period of work, paid or unpaid, to gain experience
secondment = a temporary move to another team or organisation while remaining employed
permanent contract = an employment contract with no planned end date
freelance = working for several clients rather than as a single company's employee
zero-hours contract = a contract with no guaranteed hours, called in only when needed
fixed-term contract = a contract that ends on a stated date unless renewed
casual work = irregular paid work with no expectation of ongoing hours
employment contract = the legal agreement setting out pay, duties and conditions of a job
contractual terms = the detailed rules of an employment contract, including pay, hours and notice
notice period = the time you or the employer must give before the job ends
garden leave = remaining employed and paid while being kept away from work during notice
non-compete clause = a contract term restricting work for rivals after you leave
confidentiality clause = a term forbidding the sharing of the employer's private information
job-sharing = two people splitting the duties and hours of one full-time post
compressed hours = working a full week's hours in fewer, longer days
annualised hours = a contract that sets hours for the year, with busy and quiet periods
remote working = doing your job away from the employer's premises, usually from home
hybrid working = a mix of days in the workplace and days working remotely
hot-desking = sharing desks as they become free rather than having a personal one
outsourcing = paying another firm to do work previously done in-house
offshoring = moving work to another country, usually to reduce costs
minimum wage = the lowest hourly pay the law allows for most workers
living wage = an hourly rate set higher than the legal minimum, meant to cover basic costs
glass ceiling = an invisible barrier that stops certain groups reaching top posts
glass cliff = the pattern of appointing women to leadership only when an organisation is already in crisis
burnout = exhaustion and loss of motivation after prolonged workplace stress
work-life balance = a sustainable division of time and energy between job and private life
occupational hazard = a risk that comes with a particular job
severance pay = money paid to an employee when a job ends, especially in redundancy
statutory sick pay = the legal minimum an employer must pay when you are off work because of illness
maternity leave = time off work around the birth of a child for the mother
paternity leave = time off work for a father or partner around a child's birth
parental leave = unpaid or paid time off to care for a child, available to eligible parents
unpaid leave = time away from work that is agreed but not paid
annual leave = paid holiday entitlement for a year of work
workplace pension = a retirement savings scheme arranged through the employer
fringe benefits = extras besides wages, such as meals, insurance or a travel card
perks of the job = informal extras that come with a particular role
performance-related pay = pay that rises or falls with measured results
sales commission = pay calculated as a percentage of sales or deals
take-home pay = what you actually receive after tax and other deductions
pay rise = an increase in wages or salary
pay freeze = a period when wages are not increased
gender pay gap = the difference between average pay of men and women in an organisation or economy
equal pay = the principle that people doing the same work should receive the same pay
time off in lieu = free time given instead of extra pay for additional hours worked
workload = the amount of work a person or team is expected to complete
anti-social hours = working times that clash with evenings, nights or weekends
on call = available to work if needed, often outside normal hours
occupational stress = harmful pressure caused by the demands of a job
repetitive strain injury = pain or damage from repeating the same movement at work
health and safety = rules and practices that protect people from harm at work
protective equipment = clothing or gear worn to reduce workplace injury, such as helmets or goggles
workplace bullying = repeated hostile behaviour towards someone at work
constructive dismissal = resigning because the employer has made staying intolerable, treated in law as a dismissal
unfair dismissal = being sacked without a fair reason or a fair procedure
grievance procedure = the official steps for raising a complaint at work
disciplinary procedure = the official steps an employer follows when alleging misconduct
whistleblower = a person who reports serious wrongdoing in an organisation
harassment = unwanted conduct that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment
discrimination at work = unfair treatment because of a protected characteristic such as age or disability
workplace equality = fair treatment in hiring, pay and advancement regardless of personal characteristics
reasonable adjustments = practical changes an employer must consider so a disabled person can work
resign = to leave a job by your own decision
make redundant = to end someone's job because the role is no longer needed
retire = to stop working, usually because of age or a pension
redundancy package = the pay and support offered when posts are abolished
voluntary redundancy = choosing to leave in a round of job cuts, usually with extra pay
early retirement = leaving work before the usual pension age, sometimes with a reduced pension
career break = an agreed period away from paid work, often to care for family or retrain
sabbatical = an extended period of leave, often unpaid, for study or rest, then a return to the same employer
hand in your notice = to formally tell your employer you are leaving
exit interview = a meeting when you leave, used to hear why you are going
golden handshake = a large payment to someone leaving a senior post
outplacement = support from the old employer to help redundant staff find new work
redeployment = moving staff to another job in the same organisation instead of dismissing them
downsizing = reducing the number of staff to cut costs
dismiss = to end someone's employment, typically for conduct or capability
trade union = an organisation of workers that bargains over pay and conditions
go on strike = to stop work collectively as a protest over pay or conditions
picket line = a line of striking workers outside a workplace, asking others not to enter
industrial action = collective measures by workers, including strikes and work-to-rule
collective bargaining = negotiations between unions and employers over pay and conditions for a group
shop steward = a union representative elected by workers in a particular workplace
lockout = when an employer stops workers from entering until a dispute is settled
arbitration = a binding decision on a dispute by an independent third party
work-to-rule = doing only what the contract strictly requires, as a form of protest
overtime ban = a union instruction not to work extra hours as a form of protest
labour dispute = a serious disagreement between workers and employers over work
union representative = a person chosen to speak for union members in talks with management
strike ballot = a vote among members on whether to take strike action
entrepreneurship = the activity of starting and running businesses, taking on financial risk
start-up = a newly founded company, often in technology, still finding its market
entrepreneur = a person who sets up a business and takes on its risks
business plan = a written outline of how a venture will work, cost and earn money
venture capital = investment in young companies in return for a share of ownership
seed funding = the first money used to start a company, often from founders or angels
sole trader = a person who runs a business as an individual, fully liable for debts
limited company = a firm whose owners' liability is limited to what they invested
partnership = a business owned by two or more people who share profits and liability
franchising = running outlets under another company's brand, following its rules, in return for fees
turn a profit = to earn more money than you spend in a period
break even = to make neither a loss nor a profit
cash flow = the movement of money in and out of a business
overheads = regular costs of running a business, such as rent and utilities
niche market = a small, specialised group of customers
market research = gathering information about customers and competitors before you sell
competitive advantage = a feature that lets a business outperform rivals in a market
sales pitch = a short persuasive talk aimed at winning a customer or investor
scale up = to grow a business in size while keeping the model working
file for bankruptcy = to start the legal process of being declared unable to pay your debts
insolvency = the state of being unable to pay debts as they fall due
stakeholder = anyone with an interest in an organisation, including staff, customers and neighbours
shareholder = a person or body that owns shares in a company
return on investment = the profit from money put into a venture, relative to what was spent
side hustle = paid work done besides a main job
portfolio career = earning a living from several part-time roles or clients at once
coworking space = a shared office rented by freelancers and small firms
staggered hours = a system in which staff start and finish at different times to spread demand
long-term unemployment = being out of work and looking for a job for a year or more
jobseeker = a person who is looking for paid work
underemployment = having a job that uses too few hours or too little of your skill
job security = how safe your post is from sudden loss
precarious work = insecure employment with unstable hours, pay or rights
career ladder = the sequence of more senior posts in a field
dead-end job = a post with no real chance of progress or skill growth
clock off = to record the time you finish work, often on a machine
core hours = the part of the day when flexitime staff must be at work
employment tribunal = a specialist court that hears disputes about work rights
upskilling = training existing staff in additional skills for current or future tasks
reskilling = training people for a different kind of work after their old role disappears
on-the-job training = learning a role by doing it under supervision, rather than in a classroom
